common_name: Purple Zebra Tomato (Small Purple-Red Striped Tomato)

planting.note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; stake or cage the indeterminate vine as it grows.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, staking the vine as it grows. Purple Zebra is a small, round striped tomato in the same family of striped varieties as the well-known Green Zebra, but ripening to a deep purple-red base color striped with contrasting gold-green, giving fruit an eye-catching jewel-toned appearance both on the vine and sliced on a plate. The flesh carries a bright, tangy-sweet flavor typical of striped 'zebra' tomatoes, with a bit more acidity than fully ripe solid-colored types, making it a favorite for salads and mixed heirloom tomato platters where visual variety matters. The indeterminate vine is productive over a long season; harvest once the stripe pattern and base color are both fully developed, and water evenly to reduce cracking on the thin skin.

common_name: Sweet Daisy Tomato (High-Yielding Compact Grape Tomato)

planting.note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the compact, well-branched plant benefits from a cage or stake for support.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, providing a cage or stake for support. Sweet Daisy is a modern grape tomato bred for exceptionally heavy, early, and sustained production of small, sweet, crack-resistant fruit on a compact, well-branched plant that fits well into smaller garden beds and large containers. The reliable disease tolerance and continuous fruit set through summer heat have made it a popular choice for gardeners wanting a low-maintenance, high-yield snacking tomato without the sprawling size of full-scale indeterminate vines. Harvest fruit as clusters fully color, picking regularly to keep the productive plant setting new fruit throughout a long summer season.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

common_name: Orange Marmalade Celosia (Vivid Compact Wheat-Type Celosia)

planting.note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil in full sun after frost risk passes; celosia thrives in heat and grows fastest during the hottest part of a Gulf Coast summer.

directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the weather is reliably warm. Orange Marmalade is a wheat-type celosia bred for a compact, well-branched habit and abundant slender, plumed flower spikes in a vivid, warm orange, a bright, uniform color that reads well both in the garden and in cut arrangements. Unlike the large single crested heads of cockscomb-type celosia, the wheat-type spikes are smaller and more numerous, giving a fuller, airier look to plantings and bouquets alike, and the plant blooms continuously through the heat of summer with minimal deadheading needed. Harvest stems for fresh or dried arrangements once spikes are fully colored, since the sturdy, long-lasting flowers hold their shape and color exceptionally well when air-dried.

common_name: Queen Lime Orange Zinnia (Muted Apricot-Lime Cut Flower Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; part of the popular Queen series of muted-tone cutting zinnias, valued for pairing beautifully with nearly any other flower color in mixed arrangements.

directions: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes. Queen Lime Orange is part of the trendy Queen series of muted, dusty-toned cutting zinnias that includes Queen Lime and Queen Red Lime, distinguished by a soft, warm apricot-orange base blending into lime-green tones toward the petal edges and center, giving each fully double bloom a soft, antique, watercolor-like quality prized by florists and cut-flower growers. The tall, sturdy stems and fully double, dahlia-like flower form make it an outstanding cut flower with excellent vase life, and like other zinnias it blooms continuously from summer through frost with regular deadheading. Water at the soil line rather than overhead to help reduce the powdery mildew zinnias are prone to in humid climates.

common_name: Zenith Zinnia (Large Dahlia-Flowered Mixed-Color Cutting Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into warm soil; a vigorous, disease-tolerant zinnia strain well suited to cutting-garden production through a long summer season.

directions: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes. Zenith is a large-flowered, dahlia-form zinnia strain bred for tall, sturdy stems and a vivid mix of colors spanning red, orange, pink, purple, and white, producing fully double, four- to five-inch blooms well suited to cutting gardens and market bouquet production. The vigorous, well-branched plants set a strong first flush of flowers and continue blooming steadily through summer heat with regular cutting or deadheading, and the strain shows reasonably good tolerance of the powdery mildew that troubles many zinnias in humid climates. Cut stems for arrangements just as blooms fully open for the longest vase life, and water at the soil line rather than overhead to further reduce disease pressure.
